lesson.grammar_point: passive voice for impersonal professional distance

listenings.text: I sit on maybe ten of these calls a week, and I can tell you in the first twenty seconds whether it is going to be a good one. It has nothing to do with the lawyer's English. Accent, grammar, none of that. It is whether the person tells me, at the start, how many points there are and how long this is going to take. Three points, about fifteen minutes. That is it. That one sentence changes the whole room. Everybody puts the phone down, because now they know where the conversation ends. When somebody starts straight into the first finding, with no agenda, what happens is that people begin interrupting after two minutes. They are not being rude. They are trying to work out how long they are trapped, and whether their question is going to be covered later. So they ask it now. And once the interruptions start, the call belongs to whoever talks loudest, not to the person who actually read the contract.

For years I opened every call with an apology. Sorry for my English, sorry, my English is not very good. I thought I was being polite, and honest. What I did not understand is what it does to the people listening. I was telling a room of very busy people that the next fifteen minutes might not be reliable. And they believed me. They started checking my conclusions, not because my analysis was weak, but because I had told them to. One day a colleague said: stop apologising and just tell us the agenda. So I did. Three points, about ten minutes. And the call was mine from that moment. The other thing I had to learn was silence. I used to fill every pause with sorry, sorry, one second, sorry. Now I let the silence sit while I think. Nobody has ever complained, and nobody has ever asked me to hurry up. A pause reads as somebody thinking. An apology reads as somebody who is not sure.
